bull.argument: Walmart's filing shows a business with accelerating omnichannel momentum and solid profitability. Walmart U.S. comparable sales rose 4.3% in fiscal 2026 after 4.8% in fiscal 2025, and the company states that eCommerce sales contributed approximately 4.3% to Walmart U.S. comparable sales, showing digital growth is feeding the core store base rather than cannibalizing it. Net sales grew 4.7% to $706.4 billion, and gross profit rate improved 8 basis points to 24.2%. Return on assets rose to 8.2% from 7.9%, and net income increased to $22.3 billion from $20.2 billion. The filing acknowledges pressure: operating income margin slipped to 4.2% and ROI eased to 15.1% as capital spending rose. But management frames these as deliberate investments in automation and omnichannel capacity, and the company's returns remain high relative to its asset base. The risk factors are real, yet the reported results indicate a durable franchise compounding its digital reach.

claims.claim: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales drove a meaningful share of comparable sales growth in fiscal 2026.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales positively contributed approximately 4.3% and 2.9% to comparable sales for fiscal 2026 and 2025

claims.claim: Net income rose year over year, improving return on assets.
Gross profit rate increased in fiscal 2026, driven mainly by disciplined inventory management in Walmart U.S.
claims.quote: The increase in fiscal 2026 was primarily driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, due to disciplined inventory management

bear.argument: The bull case rests on headline growth, but the filing shows the cost of that growth rising faster than the profit it produces. Operating income margin fell from 4.4% to 4.2%, and operating income rose only from $29,348 million to $29,825 million while net sales grew 4.7%. Operating expenses climbed to 20.9% of net sales from 20.7%, driven partly by roughly $0.9 billion of higher self-insured general liability claims and a $0.7 billion PhonePe share-based compensation charge. ROI fell to 15.1% from 15.5% as invested capital rose on heavier property and equipment purchases. The risk factors warn that eCommerce and AI investments will hurt financial performance in the short term, that failure to realize their benefits may hurt it longer term, and that AI-enabled platforms could pull traffic from stores. Net income growth was also helped by fair value gains on equity investments, which the MD&A itself credits for the ROA increase. Reported returns look stable only because of those non-operating items.

claims.claim: Operating income margin declined, showing profit did not keep pace with sales growth.
claims.quote: Operating income as a percentage of net sales 4.2 % 4.4 %

claims.claim: Net income gain was partly driven by fair value gains on investments, not operations alone.
claims.quote: net increases in the fair value of our equity and other investments combined with higher operating income

claims.claim: Risk factors warn that eCommerce and technology investments may hurt results in the short term and may never deliver benefits.
claims.quote: the cost of certain investments in eCommerce, technology, talent and automation, including any operating losses incurred for those initiatives, will adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term

bull.argument: The bear's strongest points are real, and I'll concede them: operating margin slipped to 4.2% from 4.4%, ROI eased to 15.1% from 15.5%, and the filing says net income was lifted by fair value gains on equity investments. But the bear overreaches. Operating income still rose to $29,825 million from $29,348 million, so the core business grew profit in absolute dollars even as margin compressed. The margin pressure is partly identified as one-time: the $0.7 billion PhonePe share-based compensation charge and the $0.9 billion rise in self-insured liability claims are specific items, not a broad deterioration. The filing also says the gross profit rate rose, and that membership income grew strongly globally. Finally, the risk factors describe investment costs as short-term drags with longer-term payoff, which is a management choice the bull case can weigh against the 4.3% eCommerce contribution to Walmart U.S. comparable sales that the bear does not dispute. The case rests on durability of growth, not on the margin line alone.

claims.claim: Operating income still grew in absolute dollars despite margin compression.
Management attributes part of the expense increase to a specific non-recurring-style charge.
claims.quote: a charge of $0.7 billion related to modification of certain share-based compensation arrangements for our PhonePe subsidiary

claims.claim: The gross profit rate increased in fiscal 2026.
claims.quote: Gross profit as a percentage of net sales ("gross profit rate") increased 8 and 40 basis points for fiscal 2026 and 2025

bear.argument: The bull's rebuttal treats two specific charges as one-time, but the filing does not label them that way. The $0.9 billion rise in self-insured general liability claims was 'influenced by rising costs to resolve claims across retail and related industries,' which describes a trend, not a single event. Depreciation also rose, and the filing ties higher purchases of property and equipment to both the operating expense increase and the ROI decline. Operating income grew only about 1.6% against 4.7% sales growth, so absolute profit growth is lagging the top line. Gross profit rate rose only 8 basis points, yet operating expenses rose 20 basis points, so the gain did not reach operating income. The 4.3% eCommerce contribution is real, but the risk factors warn that online growth may pull traffic from stores and reduce cross-store sales, and that operating losses from these investments will weigh on results. Management's ROI fell because invested capital rose faster than returns. A business whose returns are falling while it spends heavily to keep pace deserves a discount, not a premium.

claims.claim: Operating expenses rose faster than gross profit, so the margin gain did not reach operating income.
claims.quote: Operating expenses as a percentage of net sales 20.9 % 20.7 %

claims.claim: The ROI decline was tied to rising invested capital from heavier property and equipment spending.
claims.quote: The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital due to higher purchases of property and equipment.

claims.claim: Risk factors warn that eCommerce growth may reduce in-store traffic and sales.
claims.quote: could result in a reduction in the amount of traffic in our stores and clubs, which would, in turn, reduce the opportunities for cross-store or cross-club sales

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's evidence is more directly on point: the margin decline, the ROI decline tied to invested capital, and the fair value gains that flatter net income. The bull concedes these points yet leans on the one-time framing of the PhonePe charge and self-insured claims, which the bear effectively rebutted by quoting the filing's 'rising costs' language describing a trend. The bear's logic that operating expenses outpaced the gross profit gain is also a sharper argument than the bull's reliance on absolute operating income growth of about 1.6%.
